children: China’s IPO boom is turning small share allocations into large payouts for some retail investors, particularly in technology companies linked to Beijing’s push in AI and advanced industries.
Seven new IPOs this year have generated profits of more than 1,00,000 yuan ($14,900, or roughly ₹14.1 lakh) for retail investors who secured 500 shares and sold them on the first day of trading.
This is the highest number of such payouts in at least six years, as per a Bloomberg report.
Stacy Wei, who works in education in one of China’s biggest cities, was among the biggest winners. She beat odds of one in 5,525 to secure shares in last month’s Unitree Robotics IPO.

After the stock rose on its first trading day, she sold her shares for a profit of about 3,80,000 yuan, or roughly ₹53.7 lakh. The gain allowed Wei to give up a deposit she had paid for a cheaper car and buy the car she wanted instead.

Chinese traders use the term “big fat tickets” for IPO allocations that can generate more than 1,00,000 yuan for a single investor. This year has produced an unusually high number of such payouts, increasing demand for new shares even as the chances of getting an allocation have become smaller.

Technology IPOs have been a major source of the gains. Data compiled by Bloomberg show that 53 stocks that began trading in Shanghai and Shenzhen this year rose more than 350% on average on their first day, weighted by deal size.
Many of the most profitable IPOs have come from sectors including semiconductors, robotics and advanced manufacturing, which are among the industries Beijing considers strategically important.
Retail investors have been drawn to IPOs because securing an allocation can deliver quick gains even when broader stock-picking is more difficult.

Alice Wang, who received shares in the IPO of CXMT Corp. and regularly applies for new listings, said she prefers companies in “hard tech” and biotechnology because she believes they are less likely to trade below their IPO price.
The appeal of IPO gains has also grown as other investment options have weakened. Falling property prices and lower deposit rates have reduced returns from traditional ways of building wealth.

The large first-day gains have raised concerns among money managers that IPO prices are being driven by speculation rather than company fundamentals. Unitree, for example, has since fallen by more than half from the high it reached after its IPO last month.
Wei said her Unitree profit only partly offset losses she had suffered in property. She plans to put the money she does not spend on her car into safer wealth-management products.

title: ₹53 lakh in a day: How a few lucky AI-linked IPO investors made quick profits
